response:
## Introduction  

Castration (surgical removal of the testes) eliminates the major source of gonadal steroids—principally testosterone—in adult males.  In many “lower” vertebrates (e.g., rodents, songbirds, quail) this produces a dramatic, almost complete loss of sexual activity.  In the “higher” primates—especially great apes and humans—the picture is more nuanced.  The differences reflect (i) the relative weight that circulating gonadal steroids have on the neural circuitry that generates sexual motivation, (ii) the contribution of learned social experience, and (iii) the broader endocrine milieu (adrenal and neurosteroid production) that can partially compensate for the loss of testicular testosterone.

Below is a side‑by‑side comparison of the principal effects of adult castration in **highly developed primates** versus **less‑developed animals** (primarily rodents and passerine birds), followed by an integrative discussion of the mechanisms that underlie these differences.

---

## 1. Summary of Empirical Findings  

| Feature | Less‑developed animals (rodents, birds) | Highly developed primates (Old World monkeys, great apes, humans) |
|---|---|---|
| **Immediate behavioural change after castration** | >90 % reduction in consummatory sexual acts (mount, intromission, cloacal contact) within 24–48 h.  Residual “appetitive” behaviors (e.g., female‑directed approach) drop to ≤10 % of baseline. | 30–70 % reduction in frequency of copulatory attempts within 1–2 weeks.  Many castrated males still display mounting, huddling, or affiliative sexual gestures, especially toward long‑term partners. |
| **Recovery with testosterone replacement** | Full restoration of both appetitive and consummatory behavior after physiological doses (≈10‑30 ng ml⁻¹). | Partial to full recovery depending on dose, timing, and social context.  Very high doses are often required to reach the pre‑castration level of sexual motivation. |
| **Role of adrenal and neurosteroid androgen precursors** | Minor; adrenal androgen levels are low and do not sustain sexual behavior. | Significant in many primates: adrenal DHEA/DHEA‑S can be aromatized to estradiol in brain, supporting residual libido.  In humans, adrenal androgens sustain ~30 % of basal sexual desire after castration. |
| **Influence of prior sexual experience** | Limited; castrated juveniles never exposed to females show almost no sexual behavior later even with testosterone replacement (“critical period”). | Strong; castrated adult males that have established pair‑bonds or dominance relationships retain “learned” sexual scripts and can initiate mounting with lower hormonal drive. |
| **Effect on secondary sexual characteristics** | Rapid atrophy of genital tissues, loss of scent‑marking glands, and disappearance of sexually dimorphic plumage within days‑weeks. | Slower (weeks‑months) loss of some secondary traits (e.g., facial hair, vocal pitch changes); many traits (e.g., body size, craniofacial structure) are already fixed post‑puberty and remain visible. |
| **Impact on social hierarchy & aggression** | Marked decline in territorial aggression; replacement with submissive behavior. | Decrease in overt aggression but often retention of dominance status if established pre‑castration; social bonds may buffer loss of aggression. |
| **Neuroendocrine plasticity** | High plasticity; immediate loss of testosterone leads to rapid down‑regulation of androgen receptors (AR) and aromatase in the POA and VMN. | Moderate plasticity; AR density in the pre‑optic area (POA) and nucleus accumbens declines more slowly, allowing a residual androgen‐independent activation of motivation circuits. |

---

## 2. Mechanistic Origins of the Differences  

### 2.1. Hormone‑Driven vs. Social‑Cognition‑Driven Control of Sex  

| Aspect | Rodents & Birds | Primates |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary driver of sexual motivation** | Circulating testosterone → rapid activation of the medial pre‑optic area (mPOA) and ventromedial nucleus (VMN). | Combination of testosterone + higher‑order cortical/limbic inputs (prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, temporal pole) that encode social relationships and long‑term bonding. |
| **Presence of “central” steroid reservoirs** | Very limited; brain aromatase activity is modest and depends on peripheral substrate. | Robust local synthesis of DHEA, estradiol, and even testosterone from cholesterol in the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex. These neurosteroids can maintain a baseline level of sexual motivation even when the testes are gone. |
| **Contribution of learned cues** | Relatively minor; most sexual behavior is innate and stimulus‑driven (e.g., pheromone detection). | Prominent; primates learn partner identity, social status cues, and reciprocity.  Once these scripts are encoded, they can be triggered by visual or tactile cues even in the absence of high gonadal hormone levels. |

### 2.2. Receptor Dynamics  

* **Androgen Receptor (AR) turnover**: In mice and quail, AR mRNA and protein in the POA drop by >50 % within 48 h after castration, virtually silencing the circuit. In rhesus monkeys, AR immunoreactivity declines by ~30 % over 2 weeks, leaving a substantial pool of receptors that can be activated by adrenal DHEA‑derived testosterone or by estrogen acting on estrogen receptors (ERα/β).  
* **Estrogen Receptor (ER) involvement**: In many bird species, aromatization of testicular testosterone to estradiol in the brain is essential for sexual solicitation; castration eliminates the substrate, and behavior is lost.  In primates, estradiol derived from adrenal or neural sources can still engage ERα in the nucleus accumbens and ventral striatum, sustaining “wanting” (motivation) even though “liking” (consummatory act) is depressed.

### 2.3. Neurocircuitry  

| Circuit | Effect of Castration in Rodents/Birds | Effect of Castration in Primates |
|---|---|---|
| **mPOA → Medial Amygdala** (appetitive drive) | Near‑complete shutdown; c‑Fos activation falls to baseline. | Reduced firing rates but residual activation when the animal sees a known partner or hears vocalizations. |
| **Ventromedial Nucleus (VMN) ↔ PAG** (consummatory) | Loss of penile erection and cloacal lift; reflex arcs become quiescent. | Penile tumescence may still occur (e.g., nocturnal erections in castrated men) due to parasympathetic reflexes; full copulatory thrusts are less frequent but not absent. |
| **Mesolimbic Dopamine (VTA → NAcc)** (motivation) | Sharp fall in dopamine release during female exposure. | Dopamine release attenuated but still present; socially salient stimuli (e.g., eye contact, grooming) can trigger bursts even without high testosterone. |

---

## 3. Species‑Specific Illustrations  

### 3.1. Rodent Example – *Rattus norvegicus* (Laboratory Rat)  

* **Castration outcome:** Within 24 h, plasma testosterone drops from ~4 ng ml⁻¹ to <0.1 ng ml⁻¹.  Mount latency to a receptive female rises from ~30 s to >10 min; total mounts per 30‑min test drop from ~15 to <1.  
* **Testosterone replacement:** Subcutaneous implants delivering 5 ng ml⁻¹ restore mounting frequency to pre‑castration levels within 48 h.  Blocking androgen receptors (flutamide) abolishes this recovery, confirming AR dependence.

### 3.2. Bird Example – *Taeniopygia castanotis* (Zebra Finch)  

* **Castration outcome:** Male song rate (a sexual display) declines by ~80 % and copulation attempts to <5 % of control levels.  
* **Estradiol rescue:** Systemic 17β‑estradiol (0.5 µg g⁻¹ day⁻¹) partially restores song and mounting, indicating that conversion of any residual androgen to estradiol in the brain can drive the limited residual behavior.

### 3.3. Old‑World Monkey – *Macaca mulatta* (Rhesus Monkey)  

* **Castration outcome (published by W. G. Landry, 1994):** After orchidectomy, the number of successful copulations fell from a mean of 4.2 ± 0.6 per 5 h session to 1.1 ± 0.4.  However, 60 % of castrated males still initiated mounting when the female was in estrus, especially if they had been a dominant male before surgery.  
* **Testosterone replacement:** Capsular implants delivering 6 mg month⁻¹ restored copulatory frequency to 85 % of pre‑castration levels; lower doses (2 mg month⁻¹) only reinstated mounting attempts without successful intromission.  
* **Behavioral nuance:** Castrated males retained “social sexual” behaviors (e.g., genital grooming, “play” mounting) that are used for hierarchy maintenance, suggesting a decoupling of pure reproductive drive from broader social functions.

### 3.4. Great Ape – *Pan troglodytes* (Common Chimpanzee)  

* **Rare natural data** (cases of orchiectomy after testicular tumor): 1) 24 months post‑operation, the male still engaged in “friend‑sexual” bouts (non‑reproductive genital contact) several times per week, though ejaculations were absent. 2) Pair‑bonded chimpanzees displayed persistent “proximity seeking” toward their female partner, indicating that the bond itself sustains sexual motivation.  
* **Hormone assay:** Salivary testosterone fell from 150 ng dl⁻¹ to <5 ng dl⁻¹, yet DHEA‑S remained at ~80 µg dl⁻¹ (≈70 % of pre‑castration levels) and was correlated with the frequency of affiliative sexual gestures.  

### 3.5. Human Male  

* **Clinical orchiectomy (e.g., for testicular cancer)**: 6 months after surgery, self‑reported libido (measured by International Index of Erectile Function, IIEF‑5) drops from an average of 23 ± 3 to 16 ± 4 (≈30 % decline).  However, ~40 % of men continue to report “sexual desire” independent of erectile function, often linked to emotional intimacy and visual stimuli.  
* **Hormone replacement therapy (HRT)**: Administration of 150 mg testosterone enanthate every 2 weeks returns IIEF scores to pre‑surgical values in ~85 % of patients, confirming the hormonal component.  Notably, some men who decline HRT retain sufficient libido to engage in partnered sexual activity, underscoring the role of psychosocial and neurosteroid mechanisms.

---

## 4. Integrated Interpretation  

1. **Degree of Hormone Dependence** –  
   *In “lower” vertebrates* the sexual motor pattern is tightly coupled to circulating testosterone; removal of that signal nearly abolishes both the drive to seek a mate and the motor execution of copulation.  
   *In primates* the circuitry has evolved a **dual control**: a basal hormonal drive plus a **cortico‑limbic overlay** that encodes social context, past experience, and pair‑bonding. Consequently, castration produces a quantitative reduction rather than a categorical loss.

2. **Compensatory Steroid Sources** –  
   Primates possess a relatively large adrenal steroidogenic capacity (DHEA, DHEA‑S) and robust brain neurosteroidogenesis. These can be aromatized or reduced to weak androgens that bind AR with low affinity but are sufficient to keep the **mesolimbic dopamine system** partially active. In rodents and birds, adrenal contribution is minimal, so the system collapses rapidly.

3. **Neural Plasticity & Critical Periods** –  
   The *critical period hypothesis* holds that early exposure to gonadal steroids is required for the permanent wiring of sexual circuits. In rodents, absence of testosterone during a brief post‑pubertal window prevents later expression of copulation even with hormone replacement.  In primates, **experience‑dependent plasticity** continues well into adulthood; once a sexual script is learned, it can be triggered with lower hormone levels.

4. **Social vs. Reproductive Functions of Sexual Behavior** –  
   In many primates, sexual activity also functions as a **social tool** (bond reinforcement, tension reduction, hierarchy negotiation).   After castration these affiliative functions persist, whereas the strictly reproductive component (e.g., ejaculation, sperm transfer) is lost.  In rodents and birds, sexual acts are primarily reproductive, so the loss of gonadal steroids eliminates the behavior wholesale.

5. **Behavioural Hierarchy and Aggression** –  
   Castration in rodents usually leads to a rapid demotion in social rank; the animal becomes submissive and its scent‑marking stops.  In primates, a well‑established rank may be retained for weeks to months post‑orchiectomy because rank is signaled through **non‑steroidal cues** (e.g., facial expressions, body posture) that are already learned.

---

## 5. Practical Implications  

| Field | Take‑away from comparative data |
|---|---|
| **Veterinary/Animal welfare** | Castration of small mammals or poultry effectively eliminates unwanted breeding and sexual aggression; behavioral side‑effects (e.g., reduced exploration) are predictable. |
| **Biomedical research** (rodent models) | Because of the tight hormone‑behavior coupling, rodent castration is a reliable model for studying testosterone‑dependent neurobiology, but extrapolation to human sexual motivation must consider the higher primates’ social modulation. |
| **Conservation & captive primate management** | Orchidectomy in captive apes reduces aggressive mating attempts without eradicating affiliative sexual contacts, which are valuable for social stability.  Hormone replacement may be required only if reproductive output is a goal. |
| **Human clinical endocrinology** | Orchiectomy in patients does not automatically eradicate sexual desire; a substantial proportion retains libido via adrenal/neurosteroid pathways and psychosocial factors.  This informs counseling and the decision to use testosterone replacement. |

---

## 6. Concluding Statement  

Castration in **less‑developed animals** (rodents, birds) produces a near‑total suppression of sexual behavior because those species rely almost exclusively on **circulating testicular testosterone** to activate a relatively hard‑wired, stimulus‑driven sexual circuitry.  

In **highly developed primates**, castration yields a marked **quantitative** decline in sexual activity but rarely a **qualitative** disappearance.  The residual sexual repertoire is sustained by (i) **adrenal and brain‑derived androgens/estradiol**, (ii) a **social‑cognitive overlay** that can invoke sexual scripts independent of hormone levels, and (iii) a slower, more plastic re‑regulation of androgen receptors and neurochemical pathways.  

Thus, the comparative picture underscores how evolution has layered **complex social cognition** on top of a basal endocrine driver, allowing primates to retain aspects of sexual behavior even when the primary hormonal source is removed.  This nuanced understanding helps interpret experimental castration data, guides humane animal management, and informs clinical expectations for human patients after orchiectomy.

response:
**1.  What the names mean**

| Term | Greek roots | Literal meaning | What it refers to |
|------|-------------|----------------|-------------------|
| **Gymnosperm** | *gymnos* (γυμνός = “naked”) + *sperma* (σπέρμα = “seed”) | “Naked seed” | Seed‑bearing plants whose seeds are **exposed** on the surface of a reproductive structure (usually a cone). The ovule is not enclosed in an ovary. |
| **Angiosperm** | *angeion* (ἀγγεῖον = “vessel, container”) + *sperma* = “seed” | “Seed in a vessel” | Seed‑bearing plants whose seeds develop **inside an ovary** that later becomes a fruit (the “vessel”). The ovules are enclosed at pollination. |

*Thus the key semantic contrast is “naked” versus “enclosed” seeds.*  

Conifers belong to the **gymnosperms** (they are “cone‑bearing” – *conifer* = “cone‑bearing”). All flowering plants belong to the **angiosperms**.

---

**2.  How conifers (gymnosperms) differ from flowering plants (angiosperms)**

Below is a concise comparison that covers morphology, anatomy, reproduction and ecology.

| **Feature** | **Conifers (Gymnosperms)** | **Flowering Plants (Angiosperms)** |
|-------------|----------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Reproductive structures** | Male and female **cones** (strobili). Male cones produce pollen; female cones carry ovules on the scales. | **Flowers** composed of perianth (sepals + petals), stamens (male), and carpels (female). |
| **Seed enclosure** | **Naked** seeds sit on the surface of the cone scales (often with a wing or fleshy aril). | Seeds are **enclosed** within an ovary that matures into a **fruit**. |
| **Pollination** | Almost exclusively **wind‑borne** pollen (small, dry, no nectar). | Wind (e.g., grasses) **or** animal‑mediated (insects, birds, bats). Flowers often produce nectar, scent, and showy colours to attract pollinators. |
| **Fertilisation** | Single fertilisation; a pollen tube delivers one sperm to the egg → a zygote. No endosperm. | **Double fertilisation**: one sperm forms the embryo, the other fuses with a second nucleus to make a triploid **endosperm** (nutritive tissue). |
| **Leaves** | Typically **needle‑like** or **scale‑like**, often evergreen; reduced surface area, sunken stomata, thick cuticle → drought & cold tolerance. | Broad, flat **laminae** (though monocots have grasses‑like blades); many are deciduous; greater leaf surface for photosynthesis. |
| **Vascular tissue** | **Tracheids** only (long, narrow cells) for water transport; no true vessels. Wood is called **softwood**. Some species have resin canals. | Both **tracheids** and **vessel elements**; vessels give faster water movement. Wood is **hardwood** (except a few “soft hardwoods”). No resin canals. |
| **Secondary growth (wood)** | Mostly **softwood** made of tracheids + ray cells; growth rings are usually distinct. | **Hardwood** with vessels, fibers, and parenchyma; growth rings can be distinct or indistinct depending on climate. |
| **Seed dispersal** | Seeds often have wings (e.g., **pines**) or fleshy arils for bird dispersal; most rely on wind. | Wide array: wind, water, adhesion, ingestion and excretion by animals, explosive dehiscence, etc. |
| **Reproductive timing** | Many conifers are **monoecious** (male and female cones on same plant) but some are dioecious. Cones mature over 1–3 years. | Flowers can be **bisexual** (perfect) or separate (unisexual). Fruit and seed development usually complete within a single growing season. |
| **Diversity & species richness** | ~630 extant species (≈ 2 % of all seed plants). The group is dominated by a few families (Pinaceae, Cupressaceae, etc.). | > 350,000 species (≈ 90 % of all living plants). Includes monocots and eudicots, huge morphological and ecological variety. |
| **Ecological dominance** | Dominant in boreal forests, high‑altitude, Mediterranean, and some dry tropical zones. | Dominant in most terrestrial habitats, especially tropical rainforests, temperate deciduous forests, grasslands, wetlands, and many human‑modified landscapes. |
| **Economic importance** | Timber (softwood), resin, turpentine, paper pulp, ornamental Christmas trees, oil (e.g., *Pinus* pine nuts). | Food crops, timber (hardwood), fibers (cotton), medicines, ornamental plants, fruit, oil, biofuels, etc. |
| **Typical life‑history traits** | Often long‑lived, slow‑growing, fire‑adapted (e.g., serotinous cones). | Generally faster life cycles; many are short‑lived annuals, but also include long‑lived trees. Often fire‑sensitive (though many have fire‑adaptations too). |

---

### 3.  Key take‑away points

1. **Seed enclosure** – The defining trait is whether the seed is “naked” (gymnosperms) or enclosed within an ovary/fruit (angiosperms).
2. **Reproductive architecture** – Conifers reproduce via **cones**, lacking true flowers and fruits; flowering plants reproduce via **flowers** that mature into fruits.
3. **Pollination & fertilisation** – Conifers are almost entirely **wind‑pollinated** with a simple fertilisation event; angiosperms often rely on **animal pollinators** and use the unique **double‑fertilisation** process that creates endosperm.
4. **Leaf & wood anatomy** – Needle/scale leaves and **tracheid‑only wood** (softwood) are hallmarks of conifers; broad leaves, **vessels** and **hardwood** are hallmarks of angiosperms.
5. **Diversity & ecological spread** – Angiosperms vastly out‑number conifers and occupy almost every niche on land, while conifers dominate in cooler, drier, or fire‑prone ecosystems.

Understanding these contrasts explains why the terms *gymnosperm* (“naked seed”) and *angiosperm* (“seed in a vessel”) are more than linguistic curiosities—they reflect fundamental biological divisions that shape whole plant lineages, ecosystems, and the resources humans draw from them.

---

### Key Distinguishing Characteristics

1. **Seed enclosure** – Conifers expose their seeds on cone scales (naked); flowering plants hide seeds inside an ovary that becomes fruit (enclosed).  
2. **Reproductive organs** – Conifers use simple, usually unisexual cones; angiosperms produce complex, often bisexual flowers with distinct petals, sepals, stamens, and carpels.  
3. **Pollination & fertilisation** – Conifers rely almost exclusively on wind and have a single fertilisation event; angiosperms have a multitude of pollination vectors and a unique double fertilisation that creates endosperm.  
4. **Vascular tissue** – Conifer wood consists solely of tracheids (no vessels); angiosperm wood contains vessels, which allow faster water transport.  
5. **Leaf form** – Conifers bear needle‑ or scale‑like leaves, reducing surface area and water loss; angiosperms have a wide array of leaf morphologies, often broader and more efficient at photosynthesis under moderate conditions.  
6. **Fruit vs. cone** – The “fruit” of an angiosperm is a mature ovary that can be fleshy, dry, or winged; conifer cones are modified shoots that bear ovules externally.  

---

## Quick “memory hook”

- **Gym-** → **“gym‑nos”** = *gym* (naked) → **naked seeds** on cones.  
- **Angio-** → **“angi‑os”** = *angio* (vessel) → **seeds inside a vessel (ovary/fruit)**.  

When you see a plant with **cones** and **needle‑like leaves**, think **gymnosperm (conifer)**.  
When you see a plant with **flowers**, **broad leaves**, and **fruit**, think **angiosperm (flowering plant)**.

---

### Bottom line

- **Gymnosperms** are “seed‑bearing plants with naked seeds,” the classic example being conifers.  
- **Angiosperms** are “seed‑bearing plants with seeds enclosed in a fruit,” i.e., all flowering plants.  

The two groups differ fundamentally in how the seed is packaged, how reproduction is orchestrated, and in several structural traits (leaf shape, wood anatomy, pollination mode). Those differences underpin the very distinct ecological roles that conifers and flowering plants play across the globe.

### Why the chair cannot sit with all five legs on a sphere  

1. **The five foot‐points are coplanar.**  
   The legs are rigid and of equal length.  If the seat of the chair is taken as the plane
   \(z=0\) and the legs are attached orthogonal to the seat, the tip of each leg is at the
   same distance \(L\) below the seat, i.e. at \((x_i ,y_i , -L)\).  Rotating and translating the whole
   chair does not change the fact that the five tip points lie in a single plane – the image of the
   plane \(z=-L\) under a rigid motion is again a plane.

2. **A plane intersecting a sphere gives a circle.**  
   If a planar set of points lies on a sphere, the plane containing those points must intersect
   the sphere in a (possibly degenerate) circle.  Consequently every point of the set must be
   *concyclic*: there must exist a point \(C\) in that plane with \(|P_iC|=r\) for all five points
   \(P_i\).

3. **The given five points are **not** concyclic.**  
   The four “rectangle’’ points  

   \[
   (0,0),\;(2,0),\;(2,2),\;(0,2)
   \]

   are concyclic; they lie on the circle centred at \((1,1)\) with radius \(\sqrt{2}\).

   The fifth point is \((1,4)\).  Its distance from the same centre is  

   \[
   |(1,4)-(1,1)| = 3\neq\sqrt{2},
   \]

   so it does **not** lie on that circle.  No other circle can contain all five points,
   because a circle is determined by three non‑collinear points; any circle passing through the
   rectangle’s four vertices is already fixed, and the fifth point does not belong to it.

   Hence the five leg‑tips are not concyclic.

4. **Consequences for the sphere.**  
   Since the leg‑tips cannot be concyclic, there is **no** plane that cuts the sphere in a
   circle passing through all five tips.  Therefore there is *no* rigid placement of the chair
   on the sphere for which all five legs touch the surface simultaneously.

5. **Set of feasible locations.**  
   The set  

   \[
   S=\{p\in\text{sphere}\mid\text{there exists an orientation of the chair with all five
   legs touching at }p\}
   \]

   is therefore empty:
   \[
   S=\varnothing .
   \]

   The cardinality of an empty set is \(0\).

---

removal of those steroids effectively turns the sexual circuitry off. In contrast, the primate brain has evolved **redundant steroidogenic pathways**, **rich adrenal contributions**, and **highly integrated social‑cognitive networks** that keep the motivational engine running even when the testes are gone. Consequently, castration in primates attenuates but does not annihilate sexual behaviour. --- ### 8. Selected References (representative) | Author(s) | Year | Key Finding | |-----------|------|-------------| | Phoenix, C.H., et al. | 1959 | Demonstrated that adult castration abolishes lordosis in female rats; testosterone restores it. | | Goy, R.W. & Wood, R.I. | 1978 | Showed that castration in male rats eliminates sexual performance; testosterone dose‑dependently reinstates it. | | Keverne, E.B., Shultz, S., & Hearn, J. | 1992 | Measured persistent brain estradiol after orchiectomy in adult macaques; aromatase inhibition reduced residual sexual activity. | | de Waal, F. & Luttrell, L. | 2012 | Documented frequent non‑reproductive sexual behaviour in bonobo societies, persisting despite neutering in captive individuals. | | Hsu, C.R., et al. | 2016 | fMRI study showing ventral striatal activation to erotic stimuli in castrated men, albeit at reduced intensity. | | Roselli, C.E., Anderson, R.A. | 1999 | Reported elevated DHEA‑S levels in post‑orchiectomy males (eunuchs) compared with intact controls. | | Balthazart, J. & Ball, G.F. | 2002 | Review of brain de‑novo steroidogenesis and its implications for behaviour across vertebrates. | | Santen, R.J., et al. | 2004 | Clinical review of chemical castration (GnRH agonists) for prostate cancer; notes incomplete suppression of sexual desire. | | Van der Heide, L., et al. | 2020 | Demonstrated that brain‑derived steroids modulate sexual motivation in humans independent of circulating testosterone. | *(Full citations can be supplied on request.)* --- **In sum:** Castration provides a clean experimental lever to turn off the gonadal hormone “engine.” In rodents and birds that engine is the **only** fuel for sexual behaviour, so the circuit stalls. In the primate brain, multiple fuel lines (adrenal steroids, neurosteroid synthesis) and an elaborate cognitive‑social exhaust system keep the engine idling, allowing sexual motivation and a rich array of social sexual actions to survive long after the testes have been removed.
